title: Vitamin B12 Deficiency
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia and reversible neurological dysfunction. In low‑resource settings it often follows malnutrition, malabsorption or chronic infection.

sections.p: A state of insufficient cobalamin for DNA synthesis and myelin formation, diagnosed by macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils and low serum B12.
b: Serum B12 <150 pmol/L confirms deficiency
If B12 unavailable, use elevated MCV (>100 fL) plus neurological signs

sections.p: Severity is graded by haematological and neurological involvement.
b: Mild: Macrocytosis only, no symptoms
Moderate: Anaemia with fatigue, mild neuropathy
Severe: Marked anaemia, gait ataxia, cognitive change

sections.p: Identify whether the problem is dietary, malabsorptive or drug‑related.
b: Strict vegan diet – most common in low‑resource families
Ileal disease (Crohn’s, TB enteritis) – bacterial overgrowth consumes B12
Chronic use of metformin or nitrous oxide exposure – rare but possible
Pernicious anaemia – autoimmune, less common in children

sections.p: Children may present with a combination of haematological and neurological features.
b: Fatigue, pallor, tachycardia from anaemia
Glossitis, loss of appetite
Paresthesiae, loss of vibration sense, positive Romberg
Gait instability, clumsy movements, developmental regression

t.b: Detect macrocytosis and anaemia; MCV >100 fL supports diagnosis
Shows hypersegmented neutrophils and oval macro‑ovalocytes
Elevated in B12 deficiency but normal in folate deficiency
Rely on MCV, neurological exam and response to trial therapy

sections.p: Untreated deficiency can lead to irreversible neurologic damage.
b: Progressive gait ataxia
Severe peripheral neuropathy
Cognitive decline or psychosis
Cardiac high‑output failure from severe anaemia

sections.p: Replace cobalamin, treat the underlying cause and monitor response.
b: Treat malabsorption (e.g., anti‑TB therapy for ileal TB) or dietary deficiency (nutrition counselling, fortified foods)
Avoid folic acid alone – it may mask haematologic signs while neurologic injury progresses

sections.p: Monitor haematologic recovery and neurological improvement.
b: Repeat CBC after 2‑4 weeks; expect rise in reticulocyte count
Re‑assess neurological exam monthly; document gait and sensation
Educate families on animal‑source foods or fortified cereals
Screen siblings in vegan households

sections.p: Conditions that also cause macrocytosis or neuropathy.
b: Folate deficiency – macrocytosis without neurological signs, normal methylmalonic acid
Hypothyroidism – macrocytosis, but accompanied by low TSH and other systemic signs
Alcoholic neuropathy – peripheral neuropathy without anaemia

sections.p: Laboratory values may be falsely normal in early disease.
b: Serum B12 can be borderline normal in early deficiency; check MMA if doubt
MCV may remain normal in mixed iron‑deficiency and B12 deficiency

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening gait or loss of consciousness
Severe anaemia with heart failure signs
New onset seizures or profound confusion

faq.a: It ensures absorption when the gut is diseased or when oral intake is unreliable.

faq.q: Can folic acid hide B12 deficiency?
faq.a: Yes, folic acid corrects the anaemia but does not stop neurological damage.

faq.q: Is B12 deficiency common in children?
faq.a: Rare in well‑nutrioned children, but common where vegan diets, chronic gut disease or TB are prevalent.

exam: What bedside tests would you perform to differentiate B12 deficiency from folate deficiency? — Check vibration sense, Romberg, and if possible methylmalonic acid; folate deficiency lacks neuro signs.
A child on a strict vegan diet presents with macrocytic anaemia. What is your next step? — Start parenteral B12 while arranging dietary counselling; do not wait for lab confirmation.

How does ileal TB cause B12 deficiency and what investigation would you request? — TB destroys the ileal terminal region where B12‑intrinsic factor complex is absorbed; request stool AFB and abdominal imaging.
Why is high‑dose oral B12 acceptable after initial parenteral therapy? — Passive diffusion allows sufficient absorption even without intrinsic factor.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral to neurology? — New onset gait ataxia or progressive peripheral neuropathy.
Explain why giving folic acid alone to a B12‑deficient child is harmful. — It corrects the anaemia, masking the disease, while neurodegeneration continues unchecked.

In a low‑resource setting without serum B12 assay, how would you confirm the diagnosis? — Use macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils, neurological signs, and a therapeutic trial of B12; improvement confirms diagnosis.
What are the long‑term complications if B12 deficiency is missed in a toddler? — Irreversible spinal cord demyelination, cognitive delay, and persistent gait disturbance.
